case_info.scenario: A 6-year child presented with headache for 1 month and seizures followed by altered consciousness for 1 day. He had new-onset daily occipital headache for 1 month of mild to moderate severity and pulsating character. Occasionally, the headache became severe accompanied by vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia. The child had 4 to 5 episodes of generalized tonic-clonic seizures 1 day prior to admission. He remained unconscious for several hours and spontaneously regained consciousness over 24 hours. There was no history of fever, weight loss, limb weakness, vision impairment, or any strokelike illness. His birth and developmental history were unremarkable. On examination, his pulse rate was 80 beats per minute (regular) with all peripheral pulses palpable without any radio-femoral delay. His blood pressure was 170/110 mm Hg with less than 10 mm Hg difference of systolic and diastolic blood pressure in other limbs. Abdominal examination revealed abdominal bruit. Fundus examination revealed papilledema with changes of hypertensive retinopathy. He was not oriented to place and time. The cranial nerves, motor, sensory, and autonomic system examination were unremarkable. Meningeal signs were absent. There was no evidence of neurocutaneous markers. His cranial magnetic resonance imaging revealed bilateral white matter hyperintensity that was more marked in the bilateral parieto-occipital region. Ultrasound of the abdomen revealed a small right kidney and renal Doppler was suggestive of right renal-artery stenosis. His computed tomography angiography revealed short segment (3 cm) and short circumferential thickening of the descending aorta with right renal artery narrowing (Figure 1). His repeat cranial magnetic resonance imaging showed significant reduction in the white matter hyperintensities.

case_info.explanation: The correct diagnosis is Takayasu arteritis. Takayasu arteritis is a chronic granulomatous vasculitis that affects the tunica media of medium/large arteries and produces narrowing, stenosis, and aneurysmal dilatation of aorta and its branches.1In this patient, narrowing of whole length of the renal artery from its origin, involvement of ostia, and thickening of the wall of aorta favored the diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis. Atherosclerosis and fibromuscular dysplasia are the common causes of renovascular hypertension in adults and children, respectively.2Atherosclerosis is characterized by presence of atheroma at the bifurcation of the renal artery and abdominal aorta. Absence of atheroma at origin of the renal artery and narrowing of its whole length is against atherosclerosis. Fibromuscular dysplasia is a nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory vascular disease that mainly affects coronary and renal arteries. It rarely affects the aorta and involves the distal part of the renal artery and spares ostia.3Moyamoya disease is a nonatherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease that presents with supraclinoid stenosis of internal carotid arteries and produces extensive collaterals. Children present with moyamoya disease with cerebral ischemic events whereas adults may present with cerebral ischemia or intracerebral hemorrhage. Moyamoya disease may present with renovascular hypertension in 5% to 8% children and 28.8% in adults.4Moyamoya disease affects one-third of the length of the main renal artery and spares the ostia and rarely involves aorta.5 Takayasu arteritis is rarely associated with posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome. It presents with an early systemic phase characterized by malaise, myalgia, weight loss, and fever, and the late vaso-occlusive phase that manifests with stroke, syncope, limb claudication, pulselessness, hypertension, and vascular bruit. Early systemic manifestations are usually missed in children. Headache, cardiomyopathy, kidney failure, and systolic hypertension are significantly more common in children compared with adults.1The markers of inflammation-like raised C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, fibrinogen, β-2-microglobulin, haptoglobin, and orosomucoid are elevated. However, there are not diagnostic of Takayasu arteritis.1Takayasu arteritis should be suspected in any child that presents with hypertension or its complications. Diagnosis is usually based on presence of hypertension, pulse deficit or claudication, blood pressure discrepancies in limbs, bruits, and angiographic abnormalities. The updated consensus criteria for diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis requires angiographic abnormality (aneurysm/dilatation, narrowing, occlusion, or thickened arterial wall) of the aorta or its main branches, coronaries, or pulmonary arteries not because of fibromuscular dysplasia or similar causes.6Differential diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis includes giant-cell arteritis that involves large vessels in adults, medium-sized vasculitis with cross-symptomatology, like Kawasaki disease that involves coronaries, polyarteritis nodosa with mesenteric, and kidney involvement and systemic lupus erythematosus. The treatment of Takayasu arteritis includes control of hypertension, oral glucocorticoids, and immunosuppressants to control the disease activity, aspirin, and specific treatment of vaso-occlusive disease. This child showed recovery from headache and adequate control of hypertension while receiving amlodipine and an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. He was given oral corticosteroids and not offered kidney angioplasty due to poor function of the right kidney on diethylenetriamine pentaacetic acid scan. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome is rare in children, mostly seen in the setting of acute lymphocytic leukemia during the induction phase of chemotherapy or rarely during hemopoietic stem cell transplantation. Cerebral autodysregulation due to hypertension produces vasodilatation and widening of endothelial tight junctions that produces vasogenic edema, predominantly in the occipital region due to relative lack of sympathetic fibers around arteries of posterior circulation. Headaches, seizures, and altered mental status are the main clinical features.7Takayasu arteritis frequently presents with hypertension in children, which makes it an ideal setting for the development of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.

case_info.explanation: The correct diagnosis is Takayasu arteritis. Takayasu arteritis is a chronic granulomatous vasculitis that affects the tunica media of medium/large arteries and produces narrowing, stenosis, and aneurysmal dilatation of aorta and its branches.1In this patient, narrowing of whole length of the renal artery from its origin, involvement of ostia, and thickening of the wall of aorta favored the diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis. Atherosclerosis and fibromuscular dysplasia are the common causes of renovascular hypertension in adults and children, respectively.2Atherosclerosis is characterized by presence of atheroma at the bifurcation of the renal artery and abdominal aorta. Absence of atheroma at origin of the renal artery and narrowing of its whole length is against atherosclerosis. Fibromuscular dysplasia is a nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory vascular disease that mainly affects coronary and renal arteries. It rarely affects the aorta and involves the distal part of the renal artery and spares ostia.3Moyamoya disease is a nonatherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease that presents with supraclinoid stenosis of internal carotid arteries and produces extensive collaterals. Children present with moyamoya disease with cerebral ischemic events whereas adults may present with cerebral ischemia or intracerebral hemorrhage. Moyamoya disease may present with renovascular hypertension in 5% to 8% children and 28.8% in adults.4Moyamoya disease affects one-third of the length of the main renal artery and spares the ostia and rarely involves aorta.5 Takayasu arteritis is rarely associated with posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome. It presents with an early systemic phase characterized by malaise, myalgia, weight loss, and fever, and the late vaso-occlusive phase that manifests with stroke, syncope, limb claudication, pulselessness, hypertension, and vascular bruit. Early systemic manifestations are usually missed in children. Headache, cardiomyopathy, kidney failure, and systolic hypertension are significantly more common in children compared with adults.1The markers of inflammation-like raised C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, fibrinogen, β-2-microglobulin, haptoglobin, and orosomucoid are elevated. However, there are not diagnostic of Takayasu arteritis.1Takayasu arteritis should be suspected in any child that presents with hypertension or its complications. Diagnosis is usually based on presence of hypertension, pulse deficit or claudication, blood pressure discrepancies in limbs, bruits, and angiographic abnormalities. The updated consensus criteria for diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis requires angiographic abnormality (aneurysm/dilatation, narrowing, occlusion, or thickened arterial wall) of the aorta or its main branches, coronaries, or pulmonary arteries not because of fibromuscular dysplasia or similar causes.6Differential diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis includes giant-cell arteritis that involves large vessels in adults, medium-sized vasculitis with cross-symptomatology, like Kawasaki disease that involves coronaries, polyarteritis nodosa with mesenteric, and kidney involvement and systemic lupus erythematosus. The treatment of Takayasu arteritis includes control of hypertension, oral glucocorticoids, and immunosuppressants to control the disease activity, aspirin, and specific treatment of vaso-occlusive disease. This child showed recovery from headache and adequate control of hypertension while receiving amlodipine and an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. He was given oral corticosteroids and not offered kidney angioplasty due to poor function of the right kidney on diethylenetriamine pentaacetic acid scan. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome is rare in children, mostly seen in the setting of acute lymphocytic leukemia during the induction phase of chemotherapy or rarely during hemopoietic stem cell transplantation. Cerebral autodysregulation due to hypertension produces vasodilatation and widening of endothelial tight junctions that produces vasogenic edema, predominantly in the occipital region due to relative lack of sympathetic fibers around arteries of posterior circulation. Headaches, seizures, and altered mental status are the main clinical features.7Takayasu arteritis frequently presents with hypertension in children, which makes it an ideal setting for the development of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome.

   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: The correct diagnosis is Takayasu arteritis. Takayasu arteritis is a chronic granulomatous vasculitis that affects the tunica media of medium/large arteries and produces narrowing, stenosis, and aneurysmal dilatation of aorta and its branches.1In this patient, narrowing of whole length of the renal artery from its origin, involvement of ostia, and thickening of the wall of aorta favored the diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis. Atherosclerosis and fibromuscular dysplasia are the common causes of renovascular hypertension in adults and children, respectively.2Atherosclerosis is characterized by presence of atheroma at the bifurcation of the renal artery and abdominal aorta. Absence of atheroma at origin of the renal artery and narrowing of its whole length is against atherosclerosis. Fibromuscular dysplasia is a nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory vascular disease that mainly affects coronary and renal arteries. It rarely affects the aorta and involves the distal part of the renal artery and spares ostia.3Moyamoya disease is a nonatherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease that presents with supraclinoid stenosis of internal carotid arteries and produces extensive collaterals. Children present with moyamoya disease with cerebral ischemic events whereas adults may present with cerebral ischemia or intracerebral hemorrhage. Moyamoya disease may present with renovascular hypertension in 5% to 8% children and 28.8% in adults.4Moyamoya disease affects one-third of the length of the main renal artery and spares the ostia and rarely involves aorta.5 Takayasu arteritis is rarely associated with posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome. It presents with an early systemic phase characterized by malaise, myalgia, weight loss, and fever, and the late vaso-occlusive phase that manifests with stroke, syncope, limb claudication, pulselessness, hypertension, and vascular bruit. Early systemic manifestations are usually missed in children. Headache, cardiomyopathy, kidney failure, and systolic hypertension are significantly more common in children compared with adults.1The markers of inflammation-like raised C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, fibrinogen, β-2-microglobulin, haptoglobin, and orosomucoid are elevated. However, there are not diagnostic of Takayasu arteritis.1Takayasu arteritis should be suspected in any child that presents with hypertension or its complications. Diagnosis is usually based on presence of hypertension, pulse deficit or claudication, blood pressure discrepancies in limbs, bruits, and angiographic abnormalities. The updated consensus criteria for diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis requires angiographic abnormality (aneurysm/dilatation, narrowing, occlusion, or thickened arterial wall) of the aorta or its main branches, coronaries, or pulmonary arteries not because of fibromuscular dysplasia or similar causes.6Differential diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis includes giant-cell arteritis that involves large vessels in adults, medium-sized vasculitis with cross-symptomatology, like Kawasaki disease that involves coronaries, polyarteritis nodosa with mesenteric, and kidney involvement and systemic lupus erythematosus. The treatment of Takayasu arteritis includes control of hypertension, oral glucocorticoids, and immunosuppressants to control the disease activity, aspirin, and specific treatment of vaso-occlusive disease. This child showed recovery from headache and adequate control of hypertension while receiving amlodipine and an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. He was given oral corticosteroids and not offered kidney angioplasty due to poor function of the right kidney on diethylenetriamine pentaacetic acid scan. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome is rare in children, mostly seen in the setting of acute lymphocytic leukemia during the induction phase of chemotherapy or rarely during hemopoietic stem cell transplantation. Cerebral autodysregulation due to hypertension produces vasodilatation and widening of endothelial tight junctions that produces vasogenic edema, predominantly in the occipital region due to relative lack of sympathetic fibers around arteries of posterior circulation. Headaches, seizures, and altered mental status are the main clinical features.7Takayasu arteritis frequently presents with hypertension in children, which makes it an ideal setting for the development of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome.

case_info.explanation: The correct diagnosis is Takayasu arteritis. Takayasu arteritis is a chronic granulomatous vasculitis that affects the tunica media of medium/large arteries and produces narrowing, stenosis, and aneurysmal dilatation of aorta and its branches.1In this patient, narrowing of whole length of the renal artery from its origin, involvement of ostia, and thickening of the wall of aorta favored the diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis. Atherosclerosis and fibromuscular dysplasia are the common causes of renovascular hypertension in adults and children, respectively.2Atherosclerosis is characterized by presence of atheroma at the bifurcation of the renal artery and abdominal aorta. Absence of atheroma at origin of the renal artery and narrowing of its whole length is against atherosclerosis. Fibromuscular dysplasia is a nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory vascular disease that mainly affects coronary and renal arteries. It rarely affects the aorta and involves the distal part of the renal artery and spares ostia.3Moyamoya disease is a nonatherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease that presents with supraclinoid stenosis of internal carotid arteries and produces extensive collaterals. Children present with moyamoya disease with cerebral ischemic events whereas adults may present with cerebral ischemia or intracerebral hemorrhage. Moyamoya disease may present with renovascular hypertension in 5% to 8% children and 28.8% in adults.4Moyamoya disease affects one-third of the length of the main renal artery and spares the ostia and rarely involves aorta.5 Takayasu arteritis is rarely associated with posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome. It presents with an early systemic phase characterized by malaise, myalgia, weight loss, and fever, and the late vaso-occlusive phase that manifests with stroke, syncope, limb claudication, pulselessness, hypertension, and vascular bruit. Early systemic manifestations are usually missed in children. Headache, cardiomyopathy, kidney failure, and systolic hypertension are significantly more common in children compared with adults.1The markers of inflammation-like raised C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, fibrinogen, β-2-microglobulin, haptoglobin, and orosomucoid are elevated. However, there are not diagnostic of Takayasu arteritis.1Takayasu arteritis should be suspected in any child that presents with hypertension or its complications. Diagnosis is usually based on presence of hypertension, pulse deficit or claudication, blood pressure discrepancies in limbs, bruits, and angiographic abnormalities. The updated consensus criteria for diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis requires angiographic abnormality (aneurysm/dilatation, narrowing, occlusion, or thickened arterial wall) of the aorta or its main branches, coronaries, or pulmonary arteries not because of fibromuscular dysplasia or similar causes.6Differential diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis includes giant-cell arteritis that involves large vessels in adults, medium-sized vasculitis with cross-symptomatology, like Kawasaki disease that involves coronaries, polyarteritis nodosa with mesenteric, and kidney involvement and systemic lupus erythematosus. The treatment of Takayasu arteritis includes control of hypertension, oral glucocorticoids, and immunosuppressants to control the disease activity, aspirin, and specific treatment of vaso-occlusive disease. This child showed recovery from headache and adequate control of hypertension while receiving amlodipine and an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. He was given oral corticosteroids and not offered kidney angioplasty due to poor function of the right kidney on diethylenetriamine pentaacetic acid scan. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome is rare in children, mostly seen in the setting of acute lymphocytic leukemia during the induction phase of chemotherapy or rarely during hemopoietic stem cell transplantation. Cerebral autodysregulation due to hypertension produces vasodilatation and widening of endothelial tight junctions that produces vasogenic edema, predominantly in the occipital region due to relative lack of sympathetic fibers around arteries of posterior circulation. Headaches, seizures, and altered mental status are the main clinical features.7Takayasu arteritis frequently presents with hypertension in children, which makes it an ideal setting for the development of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome.

case_info.explanation: The correct diagnosis is Takayasu arteritis. Takayasu arteritis is a chronic granulomatous vasculitis that affects the tunica media of medium/large arteries and produces narrowing, stenosis, and aneurysmal dilatation of aorta and its branches.1In this patient, narrowing of whole length of the renal artery from its origin, involvement of ostia, and thickening of the wall of aorta favored the diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis. Atherosclerosis and fibromuscular dysplasia are the common causes of renovascular hypertension in adults and children, respectively.2Atherosclerosis is characterized by presence of atheroma at the bifurcation of the renal artery and abdominal aorta. Absence of atheroma at origin of the renal artery and narrowing of its whole length is against atherosclerosis. Fibromuscular dysplasia is a nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory vascular disease that mainly affects coronary and renal arteries. It rarely affects the aorta and involves the distal part of the renal artery and spares ostia.3Moyamoya disease is a nonatherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease that presents with supraclinoid stenosis of internal carotid arteries and produces extensive collaterals. Children present with moyamoya disease with cerebral ischemic events whereas adults may present with cerebral ischemia or intracerebral hemorrhage. Moyamoya disease may present with renovascular hypertension in 5% to 8% children and 28.8% in adults.4Moyamoya disease affects one-third of the length of the main renal artery and spares the ostia and rarely involves aorta.5 Takayasu arteritis is rarely associated with posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome. It presents with an early systemic phase characterized by malaise, myalgia, weight loss, and fever, and the late vaso-occlusive phase that manifests with stroke, syncope, limb claudication, pulselessness, hypertension, and vascular bruit. Early systemic manifestations are usually missed in children. Headache, cardiomyopathy, kidney failure, and systolic hypertension are significantly more common in children compared with adults.1The markers of inflammation-like raised C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, fibrinogen, β-2-microglobulin, haptoglobin, and orosomucoid are elevated. However, there are not diagnostic of Takayasu arteritis.1Takayasu arteritis should be suspected in any child that presents with hypertension or its complications. Diagnosis is usually based on presence of hypertension, pulse deficit or claudication, blood pressure discrepancies in limbs, bruits, and angiographic abnormalities. The updated consensus criteria for diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis requires angiographic abnormality (aneurysm/dilatation, narrowing, occlusion, or thickened arterial wall) of the aorta or its main branches, coronaries, or pulmonary arteries not because of fibromuscular dysplasia or similar causes.6Differential diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis includes giant-cell arteritis that involves large vessels in adults, medium-sized vasculitis with cross-symptomatology, like Kawasaki disease that involves coronaries, polyarteritis nodosa with mesenteric, and kidney involvement and systemic lupus erythematosus. The treatment of Takayasu arteritis includes control of hypertension, oral glucocorticoids, and immunosuppressants to control the disease activity, aspirin, and specific treatment of vaso-occlusive disease. This child showed recovery from headache and adequate control of hypertension while receiving amlodipine and an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. He was given oral corticosteroids and not offered kidney angioplasty due to poor function of the right kidney on diethylenetriamine pentaacetic acid scan. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome is rare in children, mostly seen in the setting of acute lymphocytic leukemia during the induction phase of chemotherapy or rarely during hemopoietic stem cell transplantation. Cerebral autodysregulation due to hypertension produces vasodilatation and widening of endothelial tight junctions that produces vasogenic edema, predominantly in the occipital region due to relative lack of sympathetic fibers around arteries of posterior circulation. case_info.explanation: The correct diagnosis is Takayasu arteritis. Takayasu arteritis is a chronic granulomatous vasculitis that affects the tunica media of medium/large arteries and produces narrowing, stenosis, and aneurysmal dilatation of aorta and its branches.1In this patient, narrowing of whole length of the renal artery from its origin, involvement of ostia, and thickening of the wall of aorta favored the diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis. Atherosclerosis and fibromuscular dysplasia are the common causes of renovascular hypertension in adults and children, respectively.2Atherosclerosis is characterized by presence of atheroma at the bifurcation of the renal artery and abdominal aorta. Absence of atheroma at origin of the renal artery and narrowing of its whole length is against atherosclerosis. Fibromuscular dysplasia is a nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory vascular disease that mainly affects coronary and renal arteries. It rarely affects the aorta and involves the distal part of the renal artery and spares ostia.3Moyamoya disease is a nonatherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease that presents with supraclinoid stenosis of internal carotid arteries and produces extensive collaterals. Children present with moyamoya disease with cerebral ischemic events whereas adults may present with cerebral ischemia or intracerebral hemorrhage. Moyamoya disease may present with renovascular hypertension in 5% to 8% children and 28.8% in adults.4Moyamoya disease affects one-third of the length of the main renal artery and spares the ostia and rarely involves aorta.5 Takayasu arteritis is rarely associated with posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome. It presents with an early systemic phase characterized by malaise, myalgia, weight loss, and fever, and the late vaso-occlusive phase that manifests with stroke, syncope, limb claudication, pulselessness, hypertension, and vascular bruit. Early systemic manifestations are usually missed in children. Headache, cardiomyopathy, kidney failure, and systolic hypertension are significantly more common in children compared with adults.1The markers of inflammation-like raised C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, fibrinogen, β-2-microglobulin, haptoglobin, and orosomucoid are elevated. However, there are not diagnostic of Takayasu arteritis.1Takayasu arteritis should be suspected in any child that presents with hypertension or its complications. Diagnosis is usually based on presence of hypertension, pulse deficit or claudication, blood pressure discrepancies in limbs, bruits, and angiographic abnormalities. The updated consensus criteria for diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis requires angiographic abnormality (aneurysm/dilatation, narrowing, occlusion, or thickened arterial wall) of the aorta or its main branches, coronaries, or pulmonary arteries not because of fibromuscular dysplasia or similar causes.6Differential diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis includes giant-cell arteritis that involves large vessels in adults, medium-sized vasculitis with cross-symptomatology, like Kawasaki disease that involves coronaries, polyarteritis nodosa with mesenteric, and kidney involvement and systemic lupus erythematosus. The treatment of Takayasu arteritis includes control of hypertension, oral glucocorticoids, and immunosuppressants to control the disease activity, aspirin, and specific treatment of vaso-occlusive disease. This child showed recovery from headache and adequate control of hypertension while receiving amlodipine and an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. He was given oral corticosteroids and not offered kidney angioplasty due to poor function of the right kidney on diethylenetriamine pentaacetic acid scan. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome is rare in children, mostly seen in the setting of acute lymphocytic leukemia during the induction phase of chemotherapy or rarely during hemopoietic stem cell transplantation. Cerebral autodysregulation due to hypertension produces vasodilatation and widening of endothelial tight junctions that produces vasogenic edema, predominantly in the occipital region due to relative lack of sympathetic fibers around arteries of posterior circulation. Headaches, seizures, and altered mental status are the main clinical features.7Takayasu arteritis frequently presents with hypertension in children, which makes it an ideal setting for the development of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome.

   Definition:

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule

   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

case_info.explanation: The correct diagnosis is Takayasu arteritis. Takayasu arteritis is a chronic granulomatous vasculitis that affects the tunica media of medium/large arteries and produces narrowing, stenosis, and aneurysmal dilatation of aorta and its branches.1In this patient, narrowing of whole length of the renal artery from its origin, involvement of ostia, and thickening of the wall of aorta favored the diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis. Atherosclerosis and fibromuscular dysplasia are the common causes of renovascular hypertension in adults and children, respectively.2Atherosclerosis is characterized by presence of atheroma at the bifurcation of the renal artery and abdominal aorta. Absence of atheroma at origin of the renal artery and narrowing of its whole length is against atherosclerosis. Fibromuscular dysplasia is a nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory vascular disease that mainly affects coronary and renal arteries. It rarely affects the aorta and involves the distal part of the renal artery and spares ostia.3Moyamoya disease is a nonatherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease that presents with supraclinoid stenosis of internal carotid arteries and produces extensive collaterals. Children present with moyamoya disease with cerebral ischemic events whereas adults may present with cerebral ischemia or intracerebral hemorrhage. Moyamoya disease may present with renovascular hypertension in 5% to 8% children and 28.8% in adults.4Moyamoya disease affects one-third of the length of the main renal artery and spares the ostia and rarely involves aorta.5 Takayasu arteritis is rarely associated with posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome. It presents with an early systemic phase characterized by malaise, myalgia, weight loss, and fever, and the late vaso-occlusive phase that manifests with stroke, syncope, limb claudication, pulselessness, hypertension, and vascular bruit. Early systemic manifestations are usually missed in children. Headache, cardiomyopathy, kidney failure, and systolic hypertension are significantly more common in children compared with adults.1The markers of inflammation-like raised C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, fibrinogen, β-2-microglobulin, haptoglobin, and orosomucoid are elevated. However, there are not diagnostic of Takayasu arteritis.1Takayasu arteritis should be suspected in any child that presents with hypertension or its complications. Diagnosis is usually based on presence of hypertension, pulse deficit or claudication, blood pressure discrepancies in limbs, bruits, and angiographic abnormalities. The updated consensus criteria for diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis requires angiographic abnormality (aneurysm/dilatation, narrowing, occlusion, or thickened arterial wall) of the aorta or its main branches, coronaries, or pulmonary arteries not because of fibromuscular dysplasia or similar causes.6Differential diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis includes giant-cell arteritis that involves large vessels in adults, medium-sized vasculitis with cross-symptomatology, like Kawasaki disease that involves coronaries, polyarteritis nodosa with mesenteric, and kidney involvement and systemic lupus erythematosus. The treatment of Takayasu arteritis includes control of hypertension, oral glucocorticoids, and immunosuppressants to control the disease activity, aspirin, and specific treatment of vaso-occlusive disease. This child showed recovery from headache and adequate control of hypertension while receiving amlodipine and an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. He was given oral corticosteroids and not offered kidney angioplasty due to poor function of the right kidney on diethylenetriamine pentaacetic acid scan. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome is rare in children, mostly seen in the setting of acute lymphocytic leukemia during the induction phase of chemotherapy or rarely during hemopoietic stem cell transplantation. Cerebral autodysregulation due to hypertension produces vasodilatation and widening of endothelial tight junctions that produces vasogenic edema, predominantly in the occipital region due to relative lack of sympathetic fibers around arteries of posterior circulation. Headaches, seizures, and altered mental status are the main clinical features.7Takayasu arteritis frequently presents with hypertension in children, which makes it an ideal setting for the development of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome.

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

case_info.explanation: The correct diagnosis is Takayasu arteritis. Takayasu arteritis is a chronic granulomatous vasculitis that affects the tunica media of medium/large arteries and produces narrowing, stenosis, and aneurysmal dilatation of aorta and its branches.1In this patient, narrowing of whole length of the renal artery from its origin, involvement of ostia, and thickening of the wall of aorta favored the diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis. Atherosclerosis and fibromuscular dysplasia are the common causes of renovascular hypertension in adults and children, respectively.2Atherosclerosis is characterized by presence of atheroma at the bifurcation of the renal artery and abdominal aorta. Absence of atheroma at origin of the renal artery and narrowing of its whole length is against atherosclerosis. Fibromuscular dysplasia is a nonatherosclerotic, noninflammatory vascular disease that mainly affects coronary and renal arteries. It rarely affects the aorta and involves the distal part of the renal artery and spares ostia.3Moyamoya disease is a nonatherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease that presents with supraclinoid stenosis of internal carotid arteries and produces extensive collaterals. Children present with moyamoya disease with cerebral ischemic events whereas adults may present with cerebral ischemia or intracerebral hemorrhage. Moyamoya disease may present with renovascular hypertension in 5% to 8% children and 28.8% in adults.4Moyamoya disease affects one-third of the length of the main renal artery and spares the ostia and rarely involves aorta.5 Takayasu arteritis is rarely associated with posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome. It presents with an early systemic phase characterized by malaise, myalgia, weight loss, and fever, and the late vaso-occlusive phase that manifests with stroke, syncope, limb claudication, pulselessness, hypertension, and vascular bruit. Early systemic manifestations are usually missed in children. Headache, cardiomyopathy, kidney failure, and systolic hypertension are significantly more common in children compared with adults.1The markers of inflammation-like raised C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, fibrinogen, β-2-microglobulin, haptoglobin, and orosomucoid are elevated. However, there are not diagnostic of Takayasu arteritis.1Takayasu arteritis should be suspected in any child that presents with hypertension or its complications. Diagnosis is usually based on presence of hypertension, pulse deficit or claudication, blood pressure discrepancies in limbs, bruits, and angiographic abnormalities. The updated consensus criteria for diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis requires angiographic abnormality (aneurysm/dilatation, narrowing, occlusion, or thickened arterial wall) of the aorta or its main branches, coronaries, or pulmonary arteries not because of fibromuscular dysplasia or similar causes.6Differential diagnosis of Takayasu arteritis includes giant-cell arteritis that involves large vessels in adults, medium-sized vasculitis with cross-symptomatology, like Kawasaki disease that involves coronaries, polyarteritis nodosa with mesenteric, and kidney involvement and systemic lupus erythematosus. The treatment of Takayasu arteritis includes control of hypertension, oral glucocorticoids, and immunosuppressants to control the disease activity, aspirin, and specific treatment of vaso-occlusive disease. This child showed recovery from headache and adequate control of hypertension while receiving amlodipine and an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. He was given oral corticosteroids and not offered kidney angioplasty due to poor function of the right kidney on diethylenetriamine pentaacetic acid scan. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome is rare in children, mostly seen in the setting of acute lymphocytic leukemia during the induction phase of chemotherapy or rarely during hemopoietic stem cell transplantation. Cerebral autodysregulation due to hypertension produces vasodilatation and widening of endothelial tight junctions that produces vasogenic edema, predominantly in the occipital region due to relative lack of sympathetic fibers around arteries of posterior circulation. Headaches, seizures, and altered mental status are the main clinical features.7Takayasu arteritis frequently presents with hypertension in children, which makes it an ideal setting for the development of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome.

4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 6-year child presented with headache for 1 month and seizures followed by altered consciousness for 1 day. He had new-onset daily occipital headache for 1 month of mild to moderate severity and pulsating character. Occasionally, the headache became severe accompanied by vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia. The child had 4 to 5 episodes of generalized tonic-clonic seizures 1 day prior to admission. He remained unconscious for several hours and spontaneously regained consciousness over 24 hours. There was no history of fever, weight loss, limb weakness, vision impairment, or any strokelike illness. His birth and developmental history were unremarkable. On examination, his pulse rate was 80 beats per minute (regular) with all peripheral pulses palpable without any radio-femoral delay. His blood pressure was 170/110 mm Hg with less than 10 mm Hg difference of systolic and diastolic blood pressure in other limbs. Abdominal examination revealed abdominal bruit. Fundus examination revealed papilledema with changes of hypertensive retinopathy. He was not oriented to place and time. The cranial nerves, motor, sensory, and autonomic system examination were unremarkable. Meningeal signs were absent. There was no evidence of neurocutaneous markers. His cranial magnetic resonance imaging revealed bilateral white matter hyperintensity that was more marked in the bilateral parieto-occipital region. Ultrasound of the abdomen revealed a small right kidney and renal Doppler was suggestive of right renal-artery stenosis. His computed tomography angiography revealed short segment (3 cm) and short circumferential thickening of the descending aorta with right renal artery narrowing (Figure 1). His repeat cranial magnetic resonance imaging showed significant reduction in the white matter hyperintensities.
